items.title: Fitch warns of growing balance-sheet strain at top nonbank mortgage firms
items.description: Fitch Ratings revised its outlooks on three major nonbank mortgage companies to negative and warned that elevated leverage and growing mortgage servicing rights (MSR) exposure are weighing on credit profiles in a higher-for-longer rate environment. In a periodic review of nine publicly rated nonbank mortgage firms released Monday, Fitch affirmed all long-term issuer default ratings but shifted the outlooks for Pennymac Financial Services , Planet Financial Group and Freedom Mortgage Holdings to negative from stable. Fitch maintained the following long-term issuer default ratings: Onity Group at B-, UWM Holdings Corp. at B+, Pennymac at BB, Planet at B, CrossCountry Mortgage at BB-, Rocket Companies at BBB-, Freedom at BB-, Finance of America at CCC and Provident Funding Associates at B. Fitch said profitability for several lenders is likely to be constrained in 2027, given a challenging rate backdrop that limits refinance volume and makes it harder for companies to retain earnings and pay down debt . That dynamic is expected to pressure leverage ratios across the sector. Three negative outlooks At Pennymac , corporate leverage has exceeded Fitch’s 1.5x downgrade trigger since the first quarter of 2026. And a failure to make meaningful progress toward reducing corporate leverage to 1.5x or less over the outlook horizon could lead to a downgrade to BB-, Fitch said. “Fitch expects profitability to be constrained in 2027 by a challenging rate environment and the lag in realizing the full impact of recent expense reduction initiatives,” Fitch stated. For Planet , the agency pointed to a significant increase in MSR exposure since 2021, as the company retained servicing from its own originations and acquired bulk portfolios. MSRs represented about 363% of company equity in the second quarter of 2026, up from 293% a year earlier and above the level of higher-rated peers, Fitch said. Planet’s corporate leverage also rose to 5.5x, up from 4.3x during the same period. Fitch considers that level high and a key constraint on the rating. The agency said it could downgrade Planet if leverage rises above its 7.0x trigger. At Freedom , corporate leverage — measured as gross nonfunding debt to tangible equity — reached Fitch’s 2.0x downgrade trigger in the second quarter, up from 1.9x at the end of 2025. Shareholder distributions exceeded earnings in the first half of the year, contributing to the increase. Fitch expects Freedom’s leverage to rise further as it grows its servicing portfolio and uses available borrowing capacity to meet potential margin calls under its hedging program. A closer look at top lenders At UWM , Fitch cited high leverage, MSR valuation risk and reliance on short-term, largely uncommitted secured funding as constraints on its rating. Corporate leverage, excluding origination funding, climbed to 5.3x in the third quarter of 2026, nearly double the 2.7x figure at the end of 2025. MSR mark-to-market volatility and a $603 million hedge loss in the second quarter have weighed on profitability. Still, Fitch pointed to a 30% adjusted EBITDA margin for the trailing 12 months through the third quarter as evidence of solid core earnings. “Fitch expects leverage to decline over time, supported by planned MSR sales and earnings above the expected $165 million annual preferred dividend. Common dividends are suspended. Even so, Fitch expects corporate leverage to remain above 2.0x over the Outlook horizon.” Regarding CCM, its acquisition of Two Harbors Investment Corp. brought $156 billion in unpaid principal balance to its servicing portfolio, along with the RoundPoint Mortgage Servicing platform’s in-house capabilities. Fitch expects the added scale and greater retention of servicing economics to improve profitability, although it does not anticipate the full integration benefits until the end of 2028. The acquisitions also drove up leverage. Corporate leverage rose to 2.9x, up from 1.2x and above Fitch’s 2.0x rating sensitivity. Fitch expects CCM to reduce leverage toward its 1.0x corporate target. Failure to bring leverage below downgrade triggers within 12 to 24 months could result in a negative rating action. At Rocket , corporate leverage stood at 1.1x in the third quarter, down from 1.4x at the end of 2025 but above the 0.5x recorded at the end of 2024, before its acquisitions of Redfin and Mr. Cooper Group . Although Rocket remains above Fitch’s 1.0x downgrade trigger, the agency expects leverage to fall below that level over the next 12 months through repayment of secured borrowings and moderate earnings retention. The pace will depend on market conditions and whether the company realizes the expected acquisition synergies, Fitch said. Related More: Fitch Ratings MSRs PennyMac Rocket Companies

items.title: Buyers Need Cheaper Homes. Airbnb Is Putting $1 Million Toward Finding New Solutions.
items.description: For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach. Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that. The company announced a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period. The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes , faster construction sides, expedited permitting , or easier financing for new homes. “Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” said Nathan Blecharczyk , Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release . While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry. The need for innovation Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly important. Realtor.com® data shows how serious the housing supply gap has become. In 2025, new-home construction fell short of household formations, pushing the U.S. housing supply gap to an estimated 4.03 million homes . This demonstrates the need for new solutions that can make it easier and more efficient to build homes. Addressing the shortage will also require evaluating and changing policies and regulations that may slow down construction and raise costs. That’s where the Realtor.com Let America Build initiative comes in. It strives to encourage discussions and solutions on the U.S. home inventory and affordability crisis. Loading... Ready for something new? Search new construction Could these types of initiatives really move the needle? Several factors are slowing down homebuilding and driving up construction costs in the U.S., and initiatives like Airbnb’s could help. “Builders cite slow permit processes, increased material expenses, and lack of skilled labor as the main factors raising construction costs,” says Michael Pearson , senior vice president of business development at A&D Mortgage LLC in Ft. Lauderdale, FL . Additionally, with expenses on the rise and the pressure to keep homes marketable and affordable, margins for contractors and developers are very low. Innovations for factory-built or modular homes, for example, could improve the situation. These homes are traditionally built homes assembled off site and delivered to a plot of land. Loading... The ongoing effort to let America build more houses is reaching new heights with Airbnb's giveaway. Bloomberg via Getty Images “While modular homes are more economical, as you don’t have to ship supplies and workers to a site build and you can better control costs and material overages, they come with logistical concerns, primarily getting the modular home on site. Innovation may find a solution that so far has not shown itself,” adds Pearson. Gay Cororaton , chief economist at MIAMI Realtors + RWorld in Miami , points out that modular homes are simply more attainable for more households. “The average price of a new manufactured home is less than $150,000, which could go up to, say, $300,000 for a double-wide home. At today's mortgage rates, for a household with $100,000 in income, that’s more affordable than a traditional home,” Cororaton explains. Still, while the Airbnb Housing Innovation Prize could turn promising ideas into realities, Pearson believes $1 million prizes won’t be enough and innovations must be part of a greater strategy where we highlight issues, communicate ideas, and have demonstrable progress. It’s also important for other organizations to jump on board. “I’d like to see more companies, nonprofits, and government agencies get involved with this kind of action. Housing safety and affordability is this issue of this generation, and together we can find solutions,” says Pearson. Robert Trent , CEO and principal at Builders Capital in Puyallup, WA , agrees with Pearson and believes the success of Airbnb’s initiative will depend on what gets built after the award. “The best-case scenario is quality homes people can afford, delivered at a lower total cost, with results that can be replicated across different communities,” Trent adds. items.title: Done right, verification gives loan officers their time back
items.description: Verification has a way of becoming the loan officer’s problem. A missing pay stub turns into an email. An employer that doesn’t respond turns into a phone call. A borrower who missed a verification request needs another reminder. And bank statements tend to be the biggest headache of all: pages go missing, borrowers send photos instead of PDFs or the statements don’t cover enough months, so the request goes out again. If income, employment and asset verification are handled through separate systems or at different stages of the loan, someone has to keep track of what was completed, what was not and what still needs to happen. Even when the underlying problem sits with an employer, vendor or data source, the loan officer is often the one who has to absorb the delay and explain it to the borrower. As more lenders move verification earlier in the workflow, often into the point of sale, it is easy to see why LOs might worry that more of that work is being pushed onto them. But moving verification earlier does not have to mean moving more work onto the LO. Done right, it can do the opposite: give loan officers reliable information sooner, reduce manual follow-up and preserve more of the time they need for borrowers, referral partners and new business. Protect the green time Loan officers know how quickly administrative work can take over a day. Individual verification tasks may be small, but together they eat into the hours an LO could spend advising borrowers, structuring deals, developing referral relationships and bringing in new business. That is the “green time” loan officers need to protect. For lenders still relying heavily on manual verification, reducing document collection is one of the clearest places to reclaim time. When borrowers can connect directly to their payroll provider, employer or financial institution, the lender can receive income, employment and asset data without asking the LO to collect every piece manually. That means fewer pay stubs to chase, fewer employer responses to track down and fewer borrower reminders to send. A direct connection to the borrower’s financial institution also solves much of the pain with bank statements because far less time is spent on things like combing through to identify and source deposits. But automation is only part of the equation. Timing matters, too. Traditionally, verifications happened after application, once a file reached processing or underwriting. More lenders are now moving those steps to the point of sale, while the borrower is already completing the application. From the LO’s perspective, that can look like more work moving closer to the borrower relationship they manage. A well-designed workflow does the opposite. When verification is built into the application experience, the borrower can complete it while already engaged in the process by connecting directly to their accounts instead of manually entering income, employment and asset information in the form fields. That gives borrowers a faster, simpler application, which makes for happier borrowers, and it gives the LO reliable information sooner without creating another request to initiate or chase later. That earlier visibility also gives the LO more time to address missing information or a financial scenario that needs a closer look before it becomes a downstream surprise. Automation still has to be connected Moving verification earlier does not help much if the workflow surrounding it is fragmented. When income, employment and assets live with different providers, the resulting data can land in disconnected systems. Loan officers and operations teams may have to toggle between platforms to confirm what’s been completed and rekey information into the loan file. This fragmentation also creates friction for borrowers, who may not know verifications are the cause, but who will certainly notice they are waiting or being asked for another document. In the worst case, that frustration costs the lender the loan. Even when borrowers stay, verification delays stretch application-to-close timelines, negatively affecting performance metrics that may factor into LO compensation and creating additional costs for the lender. A connected verification experience brings income, employment and assets into one borrower flow and syncs the resulting data back to the LOS in real time. That means fewer systems for lending teams to manage, less information to rekey and fewer separate requests for borrowers to complete, helping keep the file moving without adding more work for the LO. Direct-source data can also be refreshed when reverification is needed later in the loan cycle, without sending the borrower back through another round of document collection. The payoff for loan officers Done right, verification takes administrative work out of the loan officer’s day instead of simply moving it from one stage of the process to another. It gives LOs better information earlier, keeps borrowers moving and protects more of the green time loan officers need to serve customers and grow their businesses. Loan officers notice which lenders give them verification technology that protects their selling time and which ones expect them to work around operational friction. Daniel Esquibel is the Vice President of Mortgage at Argyle. This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. items.title: Fitch affirms Finance of America’s CCC rating as key risks, leverage persist
items.description: Finance of America Companies’ long-term credit ratings remain deep in speculative-grade territory, even as the company reduces near-term risk and improves underlying profitability, according to a review published Monday by Fitch Ratings . Fitch this week affirmed the long-term issuer default ratings of Finance of America Companies and its subsidiaries, Finance of America Equity Capital LLC and Finance of America Funding LLC, with a CCC rating and a positive outlook. Fitch also affirmed Finance of America Funding’s senior secured debt rating at CCC- with a recovery rating of RR5. Fitch defines CCC ratings as having a very low margin for safety, with default considered a real possibility. But the ratings agency also explained that it maintains a positive outlook for Finance of America (FOA) due to its "established market position within the reverse mortgage sector," along with experience senior management and support from Brian Libman, who chairs its board of directors. The action is part of Fitch's periodic peer review of nine publicly rated nonbank mortgage companies. Like other lenders, FOA has been contending with volatile interest rates , high leverage and constrained liquidity as the broader mortgage market remains cyclical and capital intensive. Earlier this month, FOA reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026 as noncash fair value adjustments offset growth in its home equity lending business. The company reported funded loan volume of $748 million from July through September, up 24% from the same period in 2025, while its year-to-date volume of $2.07 billion was up 17% year over year. The company also said during its Q3 earnings call that it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. In June 2024, FOA announced a restructuring of unsecured debt into secure notes while extending the original 2025 maturity date. That debt was restructured into two tranches, with $200 million in secured first-lien notes due in 2026 (along with an option to extend to 2027) and $150 million in exchangeable senior first-lien notes due in 2029. Why FOA's rating was affirmed In its report , Fitch said the positive outlook reflects FOA’s work over the past year to address material near-term obligations and its improved profitability when excluding fair value marks. The agency indicated it could raise FOA’s issuer default rating to B- if the company builds a “substantial” liquidity cushion beyond remaining repayment obligations and continues to de-lever through retained earnings. The ratings remain constrained by relatively weak liquidity and high leverage, a short-term and largely secured funding profile, and elevated key person risk tied to Libman. Additionally, the review factored in the highly cyclical nature of mortgage originations, as well as the volatility tied to mortgage servicing rights valuations and securitization residuals. The announcement illustrates that while FOA has taken steps to stabilize its balance sheet, its capital structure and earnings volatility still present elevated credit risk for mortgage and capital markets participants — including warehouse lenders and secondary market investors. Why the rating could shift in the future Fitch noted that its positive outlook could be revised to stable, or the CCC rating could be cut, if Finance of America fails to bolster its liquidity before upcoming maturities. Other factors that could drive a downgrade include deteriorating profitability and sustained leverage above 15s. The ratings agency said that FOA's ratio of total debt to tangible equity — excluding obligations tied to HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) and nonrecourse debt — was 33.7x at the end of September, up from 14.0x at the end of 2025. Fitch said it believes leverage will stay sensitive to interest rate movements. In December 2025, FOA issued $50 million of preferred stock to funds managed by Blue Owl Capital . Fitch treats these preferred shares as debt, since change-of-control provisions mandate redemption of the preferred shares in cash. But the agency said it does not believe the preferred shares will be a permanent part of FOA's capital structure as scheduled increases in coupons, starting with a 300-bps increase at the seventh anniversary date, provide an incentive to redeem and create an effective maturity. "We think it speaks a lot to the interest in the reverse segment, the fact that they’re willing to make an equity commitment to us and acquire the product that we’re generating," FOA CEO Graham Fleming told HousingWire 's Reverse Mortgage Daily earlier this year about the transaction. Fitch also noted potential upsides for FOA's ratings. These include sustained improvement in liquidity after near-term obligations are repaid, return on average assets being maintained above 1% with positive cash generation, and gross leverage staying below 10x. The agency also cited better funding flexibility through long-term and more committed facilities, growth that strengthens the FOA franchise brand, and deeper management expertise and clear succession planning as potential reasons to bolster the company's ratings down the road. items.title: Loudoun Supervisors Halt New Data Center Approvals For Up To One Year
items.description: The data center capital of the world is pressing pause on legislative approvals for the digital infrastructure facilities through as late as September of next year. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1, with one abstaining, Tuesday evening to halt consideration of legislative applications for data centers and substations, with a retroactive effective date of Sept. 15. Thirty-three legislative applications are currently active, according to the resolution . Loudoun County Tuesday night's Loudoun County Board of Supervisors meeting Supervisor Kristen Umstattd, who represents the Leesburg District, voted against the motion, and Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who represents the Catoctin District, abstained. "Just the fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the review that culminated in the resolution, said just before the vote. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight," added Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District. Loudoun County is in the second phase of its impact study that would establish new guidance and standards for data centers and substations. The result of that study is expected to be released next spring. The county's pause comes as communities across the U.S. are fighting to slow down the rapidly spreading asset class. Next door to Loudoun, Prince William County in September drastically shrank its map for data centers that are allowed by right. Montgomery County instituted an 18-month data center freeze in July. New York instituted a yearlong moratorium for large-scale data centers, also in July, and at least seven more states are considering similar measures, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Loudoun’s halting of legislative applications includes rezonings and special exceptions that need to be approved by the board. Administrative applications for things like site plans and subdivision plans would still be allowed to proceed. Data center moratoriums are not allowed in Virginia. But since the board has one year to review legislative applications under Loudoun's zoning ordinance, it's using that length of time to effect the pause. At Tuesday night's board meeting, Loudoun County Attorney Leo Rogers confirmed the legality of the pause that the county is undertaking, but said he does believe there is a "real threat of litigation" from data center applicants. The legislative effort dates back to July, when the supervisors asked county staff to look into whether instituting such a pause would be permissible. In September, after getting the green light from the county's attorney, the board voted to direct staff to draw up a resolution for the final vote. In March 2025, Loudoun took its first step in limiting data center development when it stripped by right zoning , requiring all data centers to go through a special exception process. Under that legislation, data centers in the works that had already been approved — 15 projects in the pipeline totaling 10.5M SF of development — can still proceed without going through that process. In 2025, Loudoun had about 53M SF of data centers, a 100% increase from five years earlier, according to county officials . items.title: Sherwood Equities Sells Hudson Yards Development Site For $100M: The N.Y. Deal Sheet
items.description: Long before Hudson Yards was the buzzy hot spot it is today, Sherwood Equities snapped up a 17K SF parcel of land at 460 10th Ave. And this week, it sold it to Joyland Group for $100M, Commercial Observer first reported . Google Maps The site at 460 10th Ave. is now slated to become housing. Sherwood had owned the residential development site since the 1990s, according to the firm’s website . It is unclear why Sherwood sold the property, but it once had plans to build more than 200 apartments on the site, according to The Real Deal . As recently as February, Sherwood agreed to add affordable housing to the site and invest $11.8M in neighborhood infrastructure upgrades in exchange for tacking on another 70K SF to the development, according to plans filed with the Department of Buildings. Now, a partnership between Joyland and Prospect Development has big plans for the site, Commercial Observer reported. The duo wants to build a 34-story, 456-unit apartment building. JLL’s Jonathan Hageman, Ethan Stanton, Andrew Scandalios, Hall Oster, Michael Mazzara and Brendan Maddigan represented Sherwood in the sale. The property had been on the market for a little over a year, according to an announcement on the brokerage’s website. TOP SALES Tishman Realty sold a 50K SF parking garage at 112 E. 16th St. to Pro-H Development for $44.3M, Crain's New York Business reported . The garage, which sits between Irving Place and Union Square East, will likely be demolished to make way for housing. Tishman representatives had filed permits to build a 22-story, 52-unit mixed-use building before the sale, with the new owner planning to turn the 52 units into for-sale homes. *** Trammell Crow Co. acquired 442 W. 18th St., a lot with a vacant two-story garage and office building, for $67.5M, PincusCo reported . The seller was family-owned Retaco Holding, which had owned the site since 1983. The new owner plans to build a 14-story mixed-use residential and commercial building. JLL’s Jonathan Hageman, Steven Rutman and Tyler Peck worked with Institutional Property Advisors’ Steven Siegel and Eric Anton to arrange the off-market deal for Retaco, Commercial Observer reported . *** Namdar Realty Group and Mason Asset Management snagged a 132K SF office building at 71 Fifth Ave. for $60.6M, PincusCo reported . Namdar and Mason borrowed $42M from Truist Bank to finance the purchase. The sellers were Madison Capital and Lubert-Adler. TOP LEASES Google Maps GFP's 520 Eighth Ave., where the Mason Tenders’ District Council Trust Funds is staying put for another 10 years Mason Tenders’ District Council Trust Funds renewed its 40K SF lease at GFP Real Estate’s 520 Eighth Ave. for another 10 years, according to a release. The organization has been in the 1926-built, 860K SF building since 2001 and plans to continue to use the property as its administrative offices. GFP’s Matthew Mandell handled the transaction in-house without any outside brokerages. *** MD Squared Property Group leased 16K SF at The Feil Organization’s 145 W. 30th St., bringing the property to 100% leased, according to a release. The deal follows Feil’s announcement that Turner School had renewed its 8K SF lease on the sixth floor of the 12-story office. Andrew Wiener represented the landlord in-house, while MD Squared represented itself. *** Nonprofit Child Center of NY inked a 16K SF lease at Stellar Management’s 35-01 36th Ave. in Astoria, Commercial Observer reported . Asking rents for the 10-year deal at the nine-story building were $50 per SF. Sholom & Zuckerbrot’s Gail Roseman represented the tenant, while NY Space Finders’ Luca DiCiero and Faisal Gilani represented the landlord. Coworking firm International Workplace Group, which signed for 8K SF in January 2025, is the building’s anchor. *** Activate Games signed a 16K SF lease at Acadia Realty Trust’s Downtown Brooklyn mall, City Point, Crain’s New York Business reported . The live-action video game experience company will occupy a ground-floor, mezzanine and lower-level space. The store is expected to open in June. Momentum Realty Group’s Chandler Slate represented the tenant. TOP FINANCING Google Maps 21-12 30th Road in Astoria, where Mega Contracting Group scored a $256.3M loan to develop hundreds of homes Mega Contracting Group scored a $256.3M construction loan for a 236-unit mixed-use project at 21-12 30th Road in Astoria, PincusCo reported . The funding came from a group of lenders including TD Bank, Enterprise Community Partners, NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development and the NYS Housing Finance Agency. The property has an alternative address of 30-37 21st St. *** Wells Fargo provided a $258.2M loan to L+M Development Partners to refinance three apartment buildings in East Harlem, PincusCo reported . The properties span 1M SF across 761 units. They are located at 1962 and 1940 First Ave. and 455 E. 102nd St. The debt retires a $232.1M Fannie Mae loan. *** Artifact and Ashok Khuban netted two refinancing loans totaling $147.5M and covering three rental buildings in Upper Manhattan, PincusCo reported . Bank of Montreal provided the financing. The first loan, valued at $94M, was for 636-646 W. 158th St. and retires a $85.5M sum. The second loan, a $53.5M sum, was for 1871-1873 and 1867 Amsterdam Ave. and replaces a $46.2M sum. The prior lender in both cases was Genesis Capital. items.title: Nvidia Tops Forecasts In First Report Without Jensen Huang, But Gets Choosier About Backing Data Centers
items.description: On paper, Nvidia’s first earnings report without Jensen Huang looked a lot like the ones with him. Almost nothing else about it did. The world’s most valuable chipmaker has spent recent weeks fighting on nearly every front — its founder’s abrupt exit, a national security probe, midterm backlash against data centers, and a Wall Street sell-off fueled by fears of an AI bubble. Its market value has fallen by roughly $2T since October to about $3.75T. Nvidia Nvidia Voyager headquarters in Santa Clara, California On Tuesday’s earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress argued that none of it has slowed the business. Asked whether Democrats’ takeover of Congress could cool artificial intelligence spending, she said customers had spent the past week asking how to get more chips and that demand will hold “not only in the ’27 perspective, but moving to the ’28 as well.” As for the turmoil at the top, “from a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. On the numbers, it was. Nvidia brought in $115.8B in revenue in the three months ending on Oct. 25, double a year earlier and nearly $7B more than Wall Street expected. Data center chips accounted for $107.6B of it. Nvidia expects about $130B this quarter, and Kress raised her forecast for next fiscal year to roughly 75% growth from 70%. Shares, which closed down 0.4% at $155.46, were up roughly 4% in after-hours trading as of 7 p.m. ET on Tuesday. In 49 minutes, one of the most anticipated earnings calls in recent memory touched on almost everything that matters to data center owners, developers, lenders and even Washington: whether demand is holding up, which projects Nvidia will help finance, who gets its scarce chips, who will run the company and whether it will keep selling to China. On China, the answer for now is no. Nvidia has stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips there, a business worth $2.4B last quarter, and its outlook assumes no China data center sales. For commercial real estate, few earnings reports matter more. Nvidia’s chips are the costliest item inside a data center, and the promise of ever more of them has sent developers racing to buy land and lock up power from the New Mexico desert to southern Ohio, a construction boom backed by an estimated $1.3T of debt . Tuesday’s report was the industry’s first look at whether the engine of the boom keeps running without the man who built it. By Kress’ account, it does. Nvidia compute “remains fully utilized across every hyperscaler and neocloud we serve,” she said. Hopper chips, now two generations old, are being rerented at up to twice their original price, and the cloud industry’s backlog has grown to $2.5T from $2T three months ago. The bigger shift was about money. Nvidia hasn’t just sold chips into the boom — it has helped pay for it , with $118B in guarantees outstanding, including $105B for OpenAI’s planned campus at SB Energy’s Ports-Pike site in Ohio. Kress said it will be “disciplined in how we commit capital” and “disciplined and selective” in backing neoclouds, the younger cloud providers that rent out its chips. “As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” she said. For developers, the fine print matters. Pressed by Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon, Kress said Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only once a project is financed, built and ready for chips. If a developer falls behind, “our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore.” Nvidia, in other words, isn’t taking on construction risk. When it does help, Kress said, a top priority will be the real estate itself — the land, the power hookup and the building shell that must exist before a single chip arrives. She called that “a great asset for anyone to hold.” Before Kress said a word, board Chair Harvey Jones closed the door that Huang had cracked open that morning, when the founder said he would be “honored” to return. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said, and would take no questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” No analyst tried. The board has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent CEO, but, Jones said, “we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” Huang resigned Thursday amid reports of a relationship with a former executive of Singapore data center firm Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China, and of alleged affairs with Nvidia employees. The board has since formed a national security and export control oversight committee. Huang is due to give closed-door testimony Dec. 1 to three House committees investigating what they called “a potential breach of our national security.” The Securities and Exchange Commission is also investigating whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday , citing people familiar with the matter. The scandal has already reached data centers. The U.S. Commerce Department first found Nvidia chips inside a Megaspeed facility in Malaysia, and on Monday, it issued a rule requiring data centers to get a license before renting advanced AI chip capacity to Chinese companies. Kress said Nvidia is still studying the rule, but “with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong.” Lenders are flinching, too. HSBC sold a $300M slice of Project Jupiter’s construction loan at prices in the mid-80s, Bloomberg reported, after Oracle sent the developer a force majeure notice . By the end, Kress sounded less like a finance chief than a coach rallying her team. “Our customers and our partners are with us,” she told analysts. “We’ve got this.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Colette Kress , Jensen Huang , Nvidia

items.title: San Francisco Hotels 'Pushed To Their Limit,' Yet Reinvestment Lags
items.description: Bisnow/Max Stein Build Group’s Julie Baccelli, CitizenM Hotels’ Eli Sokol, Marriott International’s Willis Cheng, Pankow Builders’ Mike Jones, LMNL Studios’ Jamie Shaw and Springboard Hospitality by Hotel Equities’ Pamela Janusz San Francisco’s tourism recovery is expected to bring more than 24 million visitors to the city in 2026, but hospitality executives say a shortage of modern luxury accommodations could limit the market’s ability to capitalize on growing demand. San Francisco’s roughly 35,000-room inventory has fallen behind competing gateway markets due to high renovation costs, lengthy entitlement processes and uncertainty around investment returns, according to hotel owners and investors at Bisnow’ s Bay Area Hospitality Summit. While major events, convention activity and rising hotel performance metrics are driving renewed optimism, industry leaders argued that significant capital reinvestment will be needed for the city to compete with other top-tier destinations for high-end travelers. “San Francisco’s inventory of hotels have been pushed to their limit,” said Jan Smidek, partner at San Francisco-based real estate development and investment firm JMA Ventures. “They can’t be pushed any further without triggering major code renovations and stepping up to that next level of capital investment.” The city is home to some luxury and boutique properties, but San Francisco lacks iconic five-star landmark hotels like in other premier tourism destinations, such as the Waldorf Astoria New York and Beverly Wilshire in Beverly Hills, panelists said during the Nov. 5 event at Hyatt Centric Fisherman's Wharf. Much of the city’s more than 35,000 hotel rooms have been left behind when it comes to reinvestment capital, with high construction costs, permitting challenges and uncertainty on returns due to frequent market downturns making it difficult to underwrite major hotel renovation projects in San Francisco. Assembling capital for major hotel renovations can be a challenging financial puzzle to solve in any market, but the cost environment in San Francisco provides little incentive for hotel owners to figure out how to best reinvest in their assets, said Eddie Yu, partner and head of acquisitions at Ohana Real Estate Investors, which controls more than 26,600 rooms throughout the U.S. and Mexico. As a result, the majority of hotels in the Bay Area have fallen behind despite the vast amount of wealth that’s poured into the city in recent years due to the artificial intelligence boom, Yu said. “San Francisco, from an asset quality standpoint, needs to catch up to the rest of the United States,” he said. “There's a lot of money here, and a lot of people willing to pay, but the people that own assets here manage money for public or private investors, and if you can't pinpoint when you’ll get that return on capital, it's quite hard to get those projects through.” Bisnow/Max Stein Rider Levett Bucknall’s Matthew Boone, Axis Architecture & Design’s Rory Carroll, KHP Capital Partners’ Jeff Stulmaker, Hilton’s Patrick Speer, Burton Landscape Architecture Studio’s Patrick Baldwin, Wyndham Hotels & Resorts’ Bob Walsh, Ohana Real Estate Investors’ Eddie Yu and JMA Ventures’ Jan Smidek There’s no doubt the market for additional luxury hotel properties in San Francisco exists, said Jeff Stulmaker, partner and chief investment officer for KHP Capital Partners. KHP owns The Jay at 433 Clay St., purchasing the 25-story property in 2021 for $221.5M. KHP reopened the hotel under the Marriott Autograph flag in 2023. “There is an immense amount of wealth. If you give people a great product in the right building and the right location, they're willing to pay for it,” Stulmaker said. Visitors have flocked to San Francisco throughout 2026 for business and tourism , drawn by the city’s resurgence as well as large events like the Super Bowl and FIFA World Cup. Rooms in San Francisco are expected to end 2026 with an average daily room rate of $266, up 8.5% year-over-year, and revenue per available room of $188, up 14% from the prior year. New guidance from Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office indicates an expected 25 million visitors to the city in 2027, boosting ADR to $271 and RevPAR to $195. items.title: Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009
items.description: As economic pressures continue to rise, a shocking new study has found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership has fallen 46% since 2009. TransUnion, a leader in global information and insights, released its 2027 Personal and Commercial Lines Annual Insurance Outlook on Tuesday, which focuses on what the insurance industry needs to stay profitable in a changing market. The report states that personal line underwriting has been strong throughout this year, but companies need to assess their strategies going forward as fewer people buy cars and homes , therefore reducing the pool of potential policyholders. According to the report, the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a sharp decline from 7.2% in 2009. This represents a shocking 46% decrease in the share of renters transitioning to homeownership in just 14 years. Combined with a 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors®, which stated that the median age of first-time buyers climbed from 33 to 40 in just five years, TransUnion concluded that the pool of potential policyholders is shrinking. The decrease in renters buying homes goes back to affordability and economic pressure, according to Ryan Thomson of The Assumable Guy . “Renters didn't stop wanting to own. Rates tripled and prices kept climbing, so the monthly number stopped working,” Thomson tells Realtor.com® . “In Colorado Springs, where I sell, 71% of households could afford a median-priced home in 2019. By 2023, it was 25.3%. So renters stay put. Or they move wherever the payment still works.” TransUnion also found that Florida , Texas , North Carolina , South Carolina , and Tennessee had the greatest influx of new residents between July 2025 and June 2026, with Florida gaining nearly 87,000 net-new residents. The most significant outbound migration was seen in Massachusetts , New Jersey , Illinois , New York , and California , with the Golden State alone with a net loss of 146,000 residents. Loading... The report found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a 46% decline from 7.2% in 2009. Many real estate agents are pointing to affordability as the cause for the drop. (Stock image) Getty Images This migration pattern is likely taking place as people chase affordability, looking for places that offer more space for lower costs. “A household may want a certain lifestyle, but not be able to afford it given the high costs of housing and of living in general in the area. State and local taxes may also play a role,” Cameron Walker , a real estate expert at Clever Real Estate , tells Realtor.com. “Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas may be more affordable and have lower state and local taxes.” The TransUnion report notes that the growing states all have an elevated exposure to hurricanes , severe convective storms, and other catastrophic weather compared to the states people are leaving. While the growing states are all located near the Sun Belt and generally considered more affordable than coastal states such as New York and California, the increased risks elevate costs beyond purchase price. Loading... Florida, shown above, along with Texas, Tennessee, and the Carolinas, had the highest net residence gains last year. However, the increased risk of severe weather in these states means they’re not always as affordable as they seem. (Stock image) Thomas/Adobe Stock “People may be assuming the Sun Belt states are generally affordable, and that isn't always the case,” Walker adds. “Property values are increasing in Sun Belt states because of in-migration, which increases property taxes and insurance costs, and inflates housing costs.” For insurance companies, TransUnion recommends strategies like focusing on retaining and creating more value from current customer, winning policies from competition, and combining risk mitigating and marketing efforts when discussing migration. For the housing market, improving outlooks and rebuilding the renter-to-homeowner path comes down to affordability and opportunity. “We need to increase the supply of entry-level, affordable housing. This includes promoting the construction of new housing in high-demand, high-growth communities. The industry needs to offer new financing options and improve responsibility to help new homebuyers qualify to enter the housing market,” says Walker. “People aren’t giving up their dreams of homeownership. They’re postponing them because the housing market has changed and the financial requirements to homeownership are out of the reach of many. The markets that can provide jobs and affordable housing will thrive, and gain the most, from future homeowners.”

items.title: Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home
items.description: Daniel Craig first stepped into the role of James Bond 20 years ago, and now, he has officially passed the duties along to someone new: Robert Pattinson . Craig made his 007 debut in the 2006 film “Casino Royale” and held the legendary gig for 15 years. He had originally planned to play the British spy for four films, but ended up having a successful five-movie run with “Quantum Solace” (2008), “Skyfall” (2012), “Spectre” (2015), and “No Time To Die” (2021). In addition to filming one more motion picture than he had planned, Craig, 58, has spoken out about how physically demanding it is to be James Bond. In the time between the last two films, he told The Sunday Times he was “getting old.” “I’m creaky,” he admitted in the 2019 interview. In 2024, he told The New York Times , “I find it really hard, this job, and it gets harder as I get older.” Beyond the grueling stunts and action required for each installment, the role demanded a huge time commitment that pulled Craig away from his family. Loading... Daniel Craig's reign as James Bond ended with the 2021 film "No Time to Die." It was recently announced Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role. Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Omega Loading... Craig played 007 for 15 years, an experience he said was "really hard." PIERRE-PHILIPPE MARCOU/AFP/GettyImages Loading... Toward the end of his run, Craig joked that he was getting "creaky" and was no longer up to the intense stunts and physicality required of the role. Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images “The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo” star married actress Rachel Weisz in June 2011 in an intimate New York ceremony . Together, they welcomed a daughter named Grace in September 2018. Craig also has an older daughter, Ella Loudon , 34, whom he shares with his first wife, Fiona Loudon . He’s also a stepfather to Weisz’s son, Henry Aronfsky, 20, from her former relationship with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky . Although Craig has said that he’s “not a method actor,” he described himself as a “nightmare to be with” while he’s working. “I want to go home and forget it all and just be normal and be like, 'Hey, family,' but half my brain’s at work,” he said. But having a young daughter at home has changed his approach to his career. “I don’t want to be away from home as much as I have in the past,” he explained. Craig and Weisz, who both hail from England, have called New York home for quite some time. Loading... Craig and his wife, Rachel Weisz, married in 2011 and have three children between them. Their youngest, Grace, was born in 2018. Corbis via Getty Images Loading... “I don’t want to be away from home as much as I have in the past,” Craig admitted not long after the couple welcomed Grace. The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images Loading... After selling their Brooklyn brownstone earlier this year, Weisz and Craig still have homes in upstate New York and London. Photo by Simon Bruty/Anychance/Getty Images In April of this year, they sold their Brooklyn brownstone for $11.8 million. They had picked it up for $6.75 million in 2018. Built in 1901, the 6,600-square-foot abode spans five levels, which are accessible by elevator. It included a roof deck, a patio, and a backyard garden. The six-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom residence was damaged by a fire in 2016, before the couple snapped it up. According to Architectural Digest , the previous owner, novelist Martin Amis , had transformed the home into a “clean, blank slate” in light of the damage, and Craig and Weisz put their own spin on it in the nearly eight years they lived there. The off-market transaction came just a year after the couple sold an adjacent townhouse for $4.05 million. They still hold ties to the Empire State, with an upstate retreat in Marbletown, NY , that Weisz purchased for $2.1 million in 2008. Nestled on an idyllic 124-acre parcel, the 2,500-square-foot stone home dates to 1785 and includes four bedrooms and three bathrooms. Overseas, Craig and Weisz have a $4.2 million Victorian mansion in a conservation area in North London. It was a home the “Vladimir” actress had purchased before they were married. According to the Daily Mail , they sought to heavily renovate the 1840 home in 2023, but had to alter their plans when an objection claimed the proposal would clash with the home’s original style. items.title: Anne Hathaway Welcomes Her Third Child With Husband Adam Shulman
items.description: Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway and her husband, Adam Shulman . It appears the couple have welcomed their third child , after "The Devil Wears Prada" actress was spotted with a newborn in New York City on Nov. 17. The photos, shared first by TMZ , depict Hathaway, 44, strolling around her hometown with a friend, and an infant snuggled up into a baby carrier. The actress first shared news of her pregnancy in June, revealing a growing baby bump in an Instagram video captioned , "Baby, I'm yours." Hathaway and Shulman are also parents to two sons: Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman , 10, and Jack Shulman , 7. Shortly after sharing the news, Hathaway appeared on "Late Night With Seth Meyers," and said that so far, the experience of a third pregnancy had been "amazing." Loading... Anne Hathaway first shared the news of her pregnancy in a sweet Instagram post in June. Instagram Loading... This is baby number three for Hathaway and her husband, Adam Shulman, who already have two sons named Jonathan and Jack. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images She noted that she and her jewelry designer husband were surprised to learn they had another bundle of joy on the way. "I mean, we knew what we were doing, but we were so shocked it worked," she revealed on the talk show. "We were so shocked it went this way, so we're calling this one our buzzer-beater," she joked. According to a People magazine source , up until the announcement, Hathaway had worked diligently to keep the news of her pregnancy a secret during "The Devil Wears Prada 2" press tour. "She wanted to reveal the pregnancy on her own terms. The press tour was about celebrating the movie and getting fans excited to see it," shared the source. Press tours for "Verity" and "The Odyssey" have kept Hathaway busy shortly in the time since, but according to the source, she was able to "focus on family" and soak up "a little downtime" in the time between the films. "She's grateful for where she is in her career and for the opportunity to be part of a film that means so much to so many people. Complaining just isn't Anne. She approaches things with gratitude and professionalism, and that's exactly how she handled the press tour," the source added. Although Hathaway is a longtime New Yorker who originally hailed from New Jersey , the family primarily resides in an Ojai, CA , home the couple purchased for $3.6 million in 2014. The couple told Architectural Digest that it was love at first sight with the property, and they knew they had to have it from the moment they first viewed it—even if it needed a handful of updates. "It was the ideal combination of romance and great design," Hathaway said. "Our initial instinct was that this was going to be a very important place in our lives. I could really see raising a family here." The 3,400-square foot home has a gorgeous Swiss chalet-inspired aesthetic that's been customized after the couple spent years renovating the home. According to a previous listing, the home had four bedrooms and four bedrooms. However, records indicate that Hathaway and Shulman also purchased a parcel of land next to the property, so there's a good chance they may have expanded the home. Based on the baby's first public outing, it seems that they may be splitting their time between the Sunshine State and the East Coast. The "Princess Diaries" actress has previously shared glimpses of her personal life, explaining that she really lives for simple pleasures. "I still get the paper delivered every day, and I love sitting down with it," she told People magazine in an interview for her "World's Most Beautiful" cover story. She explained that on a slow day, she loves cuddling with the family's new puppy and finding time to speak to loved ones. "I'm always zipping from one thing to another," she admitted. "I'd love to have breakfast with a friend. I'd love to go for a walk, maybe do a little window shopping, maybe go to a museum. I'm very meandering on my days off." In the interview, she also shared her appreciation for Shulman, noting that he "supports" her "completely," especially in a year as busy as the one she's having now. "I'm so lucky that he's my partner that I spend my life with. If I didn't know that before this past year, I think I really know it now, because with absolutely everything, he's just, he's on it. He holds it down," she gushed. "I hope that doesn't sound like I'm bragging, but he's a dream partner to me." items.title: Why 2027 may turn into a land negotiation year for homebuilders
items.description: In the early ’90s, I worked in Wells Fargo Bank ’s real estate workout group in Southern California. The aerospace collapse was crushing the local economy; Los Angeles County alone lost 400,000 jobs. Roughly 25% of WFB’s assets were in commercial real estate (including homebuilding), and another 25% in home mortgages, mostly in California. That was half the bank. Writing off loans and walking away to clean up the books wasn’t an option; we lacked the capital. So we fought for every penny. We asked for re-margins early on, short-term extensions and collected from borrowers before they ran out of money. We pursued personal guarantees and were willing to fight for them. I realize it is not what an audience of builders wants to hear, but everyone fights to survive. Bank of America was in a different position. It had less real estate concentration and wanted to expand by buying distressed banks, but it couldn’t until regulators were convinced it had moved past its own problems. So BofA cut deals or foreclosed, cleaning house. Its real estate recovery rate was far lower than ours. That doesn’t mean BofA was wrong. It simply had different incentives. Everyone knows Charlie Munger’s line, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.” We tend to apply it to individuals. But the coming year will be driven largely by company incentives. If you’re a builder, understanding the incentives of the companies across the table may be the most valuable market intelligence you can gather. Why the coming year? As I’ve said before, I’m not a big fan of short-term market projections. Over longer time spans, demographics , the fundamental balance of supply and demand, and affordability play out; they’re directionally predictable, if not precise. The short term has so many unforeseeable temporary factors that it can, paradoxically, be harder to call. Strategy is for the long term; in the short run, it’s mostly tactics, adapting to what’s in front of you. But caution about predicting short-term conditions is different from dismissing contingency planning. Housing market conditions have clearly deteriorated. Whatever the cause (war, politics, rising rates or all of the above), I suspect we never had the correction we should have after rates spiked in ’22. A frozen-in-place resale market and the effectiveness of rate buydowns made the following years difficult, but less so than many of us expected. One of the most intriguing aspects is that I can’t recall a more difficult period in homebuilding (to be clear, I’ve been through far worse, twice) that had so little impact on the land market. The reason was the belief that land was in such short supply that builders couldn’t afford to give up what they had and would need to buy more. Builders weren’t staying in current deals because they necessarily made sense, nor were they buying new ones because they liked the prices. The attitude was: what’s the alternative? That belief rested on two assumptions. First, that today’s weakness is a short-term problem: the rate shock would wear off, and buying would pick up. Second, that long-term fundamentals hadn’t changed, so demand would rebound and buoy prices. Either could prove true, but I’m skeptical. As I’ve written over the past year, future demand looks weak relative to the past, not a temporary dip but the start of a regime change. Once that becomes conventional wisdom, why would builders feel the need to control six to seven years of lots? Remember when three to four was considered plenty? Why won’t that be the case again? The land demand rotation I think 2027 is the year land prices will correct, not just terms but real prices. It’s current economics meeting a dawning recognition that the future will need fewer lots. Beyond a few year-end closings, not much will happen in the rest of 2026, and some will wait to see whether a magic spring rebound arrives. But over the last few months, we’ve seen a sharp downgrade in builder expectations for next year. Few expect things to improve soon. The public builders reinforce this. Many are eliminating forecasts or revising unit counts downward. Much like the difference between making a dollar and losing a dollar, which is much bigger than two dollars, once a builder admits it won’t be growing, it becomes much easier to walk from some positions. Once that threshold is crossed, Wall Street cares far less whether a builder shrinks 2% or 6%. Reasonable people can differ on this; there are multiple paths forward. But I think the odds are high enough to warrant contingency planning. If I’m right, what happens? To start, many land bankers (not the old vets, but the newcomers) will learn they weren’t offering a credit product. Like it or not, they’re in real estate and have taken real estate risk. Too many fundamentals in that business were stretched on the belief that big builders wouldn’t walk en masse . Expect meaningful re-trades, not just extensions. Meanwhile, land sellers will hear builders say they have options and don’t need to rush: “We’ll pay less and take them down on a rolling schedule with a 3% annual escalator. We can’t pay a land banker 10% to hold them; the margin’s too thin.” That’s where incentives come in. How each negotiation goes will depend heavily on the incentives of the companies involved, and each company has multiple layers. Using land bankers as an example, here are a few questions worth addressing. How are their asset management fees calculated and collected? As a percentage of revenue, assets (write-downs matter), or cost? Are they amortized over the deal’s life, or literally eat-what-you-kill, paid at closing? Last cycle, it wasn’t uncommon for equity funds to earn asset management fees based on revenue, with half taken up front and the rest amortized over the deal’s projected life. items.title: Guild's Nora Guerra on helping baby boomers buy and rehab homes with reverse mortgages
items.description: Baby boomers represent 42% of homebuyers and 55% of sellers, according to the most recent data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), yet the mortgage industry has yet to fully account for their presence. That was the message shared last week by Nora Guerra, senior vice president of community lending solutions at Guild Mortgage , during the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)'s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio. Guerra — who previously worked at Freddie Mac , where she studied how homebuyers change by age group — told the audience that lenders have spent years chasing younger consumers while overlooking older, equity-rich groups who are moving frequently and are in need of help. "This 55-plus buyer, it's a main demographic buyer. Everybody has been so focused on the millennial — the older millennial, the younger millennial — and now the Gen Zer ," she said. Jolted by the pandemic Before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, boomers were largely staying put and had few incentives to move, Guerra said. But that changed quickly as single-family home price appreciation skyrocketed from 3.2% in 2019 to 11.3% in 2021 and 11.9% in 2022, according to HousingWire Data . That contributed heavily to home equity accumulation, with homeowners 62 and older now holding $15.34 trillion in housing wealth, according to NRMLA and RiskSpan . Additionally, the pandemic caused a rupture in many families' living situations. "They were sheltered in place. They couldn't see their loved ones, their grandchildren and their children, and it shook them very hard," Guerra said. Across years of research, Guerra has uncovered four distinct groups of older homebuyers: Family-focused movers who want to be closer to children, grandchildren and other family members Lifestyle-focused retirees, who seek to fulfill daily routines and may be strong candidates for renovation loans Financial-focused planners, who want their housing decisions to align with long-term plans like retirement Stay-put homeowners, who want to age in place in a familiar community but have hurdles to doing so Each of these groups are likely to need financing to accomplish their goals, she said. Reverse mortgages may offer a more cost-effective solution since they don't require a monthly payment, and they're often a fit for applicants who've been turned down for other types of mortgage credit. Reverse mortgage for purchase programs , in particular, can fulfill their needs. These products allow seniors to sell their current home and use the equity to buy a similar or more expensive property without monthly payments or the need to pay in cash. "They really don't know what options are out there, so they feel no one wants to finance me," Guerra remarked. According to NAR research cited by Guerra, senior homebuyers frequently utilize mortgages, but the trend wanes as the buyer grows older. The data shows that among 61- to 70-year-olds, 61% financed their purchase during the year ending in June 2025. The percentage dropped to 54% among 71- to 79-year-olds, and to 48% among those 80 and older. Focus on solutions, not challenges Guerra said mortgage professionals spend too much time discussing problems and not enough time on finding or developing solutions. This can be particularly unhelpful when working with house-rich, cash-poor clients who have significant equity but little in the way of savings or retirement funds. With these types of needs-based borrowers, reverse mortgage professionals should be asking about the cash they're looking to access for both everyday living expenses and unexpected expenses . Develop a cash-flow plan based on what they have in their retirement accounts and other investments. Whether a client is considering a federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage or a proprietary reverse mortgage, counselors certified by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are a key resource to tap into. Guerra said she works with more than 200 counselors nationwide who "help educate and hold the hand of your parent, and tell them all about this program and how it works." Originators should ask direct questions about the client's preferences to pay for their next home, identify any assets they don't want to touch for that purpose, and offer comparisons of what the financial results will look like with a reverse mortgage versus a cash deal. Family members often fear there will be nothing left for them when their parent or grandparent dies. But planning ahead of time can help heirs to sell the home and keep any proceeds, or to repay the reverse mortgage and continue living there. Some lenders offer private-label solutions for these exact situations . Guerra also pointed to NAR data showing that 14% of recent home purchases were tied to multigenerational living situations. These clients often need their family involved when making decisions about reverse mortgages. Adult children want to protect their parents' assets, so originators should include relatives early in the process. "Mom and dad haven't bought a home in the last 10 or 15 years due to lack of inventory. Grandma and grandpa haven't bought a home in the last 15 to 20 years due to the same reason," Guerra told the audience. "Multigenerational living is what we're seeing on these 1003 (loan applications) — lots of grandparents cosigning for their millennial and Gen Z grandchildren if they can afford it, but also lots of gift letters." items.title: Congress Puts Up $216M For Energy Department Relocation From Forrestal
items.description: The Department of Energy’s 1.8M SF office complex along Independence Avenue is one step closer to its next chapter. A Senate committee approved $215.6M in funding Wednesday to relocate the agency’s employees from the James V. Forrestal trio of office buildings into its next headquarters. The funds can be used to prepare Forrestal for disposition and Energy's new headquarters for its habitation, according to a resolution from the Senate’s Environment and Public Works Committee. The 1960s-era Forrestal complex at 1000 Independence Ave. SW acts as a massive physical barrier between the National Mall and the Wharf. Its redevelopment has long been viewed by urban planners as a key component in unlocking a mixed-use vision for D.C.'s southwest federal corridor. Google Maps The Department of Energy's James V. Forrestal Building at 1000 Independence Ave. SW The funding will go to the federal government’s landlord, the General Services Administration , via its FY2026 Optimization Program Prospectus. The EPW Committee passed that prospectus Wednesday, and a House panel approved the funding in July . The GSA announced in March that Energy would be clearing out of Forrestal and moving into the Department of Education’s 50-year-old headquarters: the Lyndon B. Johnson Building on Maryland Avenue Southwest. Education, in turn, announced that it would move into a building at 500 D St. SW, which was previously leased for the now largely defunct U.S. Agency for International Development. That move, expected to cut Education's footprint by 80%, was set to be completed in August. The GSA said in a Wednesday news release that the relocation money allows the agency “to consider alternative uses for the Forrestal Building, including disposition.” The GSA didn’t provide a timeline for when the move will begin or how long it should take. Its press office didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for information. GSA Administrator Edward Forst said in the release that the move will “reduce waste, avoid more than $350 million in delinquent maintenance costs, and deliver a workplace that better serves agencies, employees, and the American taxpayer.” In September, a Government Accountability Office report said the agency would need funding to “fit out classified space to meet Energy’s mission needs” at its new LBJ Building home. Momentum has been building over the past two years to transform the 230 acres that make up D.C.’s southwest federal corridor into a new mixed-use neighborhood. The federal government this year offloaded its first two federal properties in the corridor : the Regional Office Building and the Liberty Loan Building on the Tidal Basin. It has earmarked other large headquarters buildings for disposition but this summer seemed to quietly pull back on those efforts, the Washington Business Journal reported . Public and private stakeholders have worried about the lack of a coherent vision and plan for the neighborhood. The first sign that a formal planning document was underway came last month when Diane Sullivan, the acting executive director of the National Capital Planning Commission, presented a preliminary vision for the neighborhood, broken into three districts, each with a distinct focus: residential, arts and culture, and federal office. Under that vision, Forrestal, which sits across from the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building, would be included in the 10th Street Cultural/Entertainment District. items.title: British Land Ups Guidance As AI Drives Restructure And Possible Job Losses
items.description: Courtesy of Oxford Properties British Land's Jo McNamara British Land has upgraded its full-year earnings guidance after delivering 12% like-for-like rental growth in the first half, as its new chief executive looks to use artificial intelligence and automation to reshape the business and reduce costs. The FTSE 100 landlord reported underlying profit of £166M for the six months to 30 September, up 7% year-on year, while underlying earnings per share increased 5% to 16.1p. The company raised its full-year underlying EPS guidance to 31p, representing 7% annual growth, from previous guidance of at least 30.5p. However, alongside the improved performance, British Land Chief Executive Jo McNamara signalled a significant change in how the 170-year-old property company operates, with technology and AI expected to play an increasingly important role. “We are already beginning to see how AI, automation and better use of data can change the way businesses operate, and I want British Land to lean into that opportunity,” McNamara said at the results. The company has begun an organisational restructure intended to create a leaner business with clearer accountability, targeting annualised savings of £5M to £7M from financial year 2028, with British Land consulting on potential job cuts across its approximately 600-strong workforce. “This is not simply about taking cost out of the business. It is about amplifying judgement, enhancing productivity and reducing lower-value activity, freeing our people to spend more of their time with customers, on our assets and on the activities that create the most value,” McNamara added. British Land's campuses division recorded 25% like-for-like net rental growth, while retail and London urban logistics grew 2% and, across the portfolio, occupancy stood at 96%. The company completed lettings covering 1.4M SF during the period, at rents 8% ahead of previous passing rents and 10% above estimated rental value. A further 1.1M SF was under offer at rents 12% above ERV, the company said. The company also completed £765M of capital transactions, including £247M of disposals at a net initial yield of 4.7%, broadly in line with book value, while a further £328M of disposals had been exchanged or were under offer. Its portfolio valuation increased 1.5% during the half to £10.47B, while its loan-to-value ratio edged up to 40%, from 39.2% at the end of March. items.title: Triten Starts Speculative, Small-Bay Industrial Project
items.description: Houston-based Triten Real Estate Partners broke ground on a 173K SF industrial project in Southwest Houston, saying proximity to rooftops is becoming as important as proximity to highways. Courtesy of Triten Real Estate Partners A rendering of Southwest Houston Industrial Center Southwest Houston Industrial Center will be on an 18-acre site at 12911 Zavalla St., near Fort Bend County in Houston's growing southwest suburbs. The speculative two-building development will target small-bay and last-mile businesses. Building 1 will be a 75K SF rear-load facility designed for businesses with warehouse and customer-facing needs, like flooring and building material suppliers or home improvement companies. The 97K SF front-load Building 2 will be tailored to distribution, fulfillment and last-mile operations. “This pocket of Southwest Houston combines population density, rooftop growth, and regional connectivity in a way that's hard to replicate,” Will Hedges , managing partner of the industrial platform for Triten, said in a statement. “Small-bay users have largely been overlooked by recent development, and we saw an opportunity to create something specifically for them.” The Houston industrial development pipeline in the third quarter consisted of 90 projects totaling 18.4M SF, coming out to an average project size of about 204K SF, according to CBRE’s report . The pipeline’s prelease rate was 31%. The most active submarkets for both construction and deliveries were the North and Northwest, with more than 1.5M SF of deliveries each. The Southwest submarket ranked last of the six submarkets, with just 224K SF of deliveries in the third quarter, CBRE data shows. The Southwest Houston Industrial Center project team includes Angler Construction , Grey Wolf Engineering and Method Architecture . Southside Bank is providing construction financing. Completion is anticipated in summer 2027. Garret Geaccone, Heath Donica and Danielle Rothchild with Stream Realty Partners are handling leasing and sales opportunities. items.title: 'Doesn't Look Good': October CRE Sales Volume Slumps, Setting Up Weak Q4
items.description: Commercial real estate sales volume took a dive in October after a strong third quarter, new data from MSCI and Altus Group shows. Unsplash/Clay LeConey CRE transaction volume totaled $35.4B in October, down 51% from last year, according to preliminary volume pricing data from MSCI released Wednesday. The last few months have included shake-ups to the capital markets landscape that are testing the resilience of CRE demand after what has until now been a relatively strong year for dealmaking across the asset class. Revisions to previously reported third-quarter data put transaction volume in the prior three months at $160.6B, up 16% from the prior year. There were no large mergers or entity deals in the quarter, which had boosted net sales volume in previous months. “There is still time for some improvement, especially as December is roughly 15% of the full year,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a note to investors Wednesday morning, noting that December typically sees outsized transaction activity. “But again, the start to the quarter doesn’t look good.” The average cap rate for all transactions was 6.85% in October, up 15 basis points from September. Retail saw the largest swing in cap rates, with a 16-basis-point push upward to 7.20%, while office was up 9 basis points to 7.46%, apartments ticked up 7 basis points to 8.22% and industrial assets saw cap rates rise 3 basis points to 6.6%, according to MSCI. Buyers and sellers seem to be quickly adjusting to the interest rate environment, and fundamentals still look broadly solid, the JPMorgan analysts wrote. The MSCI data comes as a third-quarter report from Altus Group, the maker of the ubiquitous CRE software Argus, released Wednesday showed momentum had been building in capital markets. Transaction volume by dollars spent was up 19.7% quarter-over-quarter and 20.3% year-over-year, with the number of properties sold also up by 3.8% and 6.9%, respectively, according to the report . The median price per square foot across all asset types was up 2.3% from the second quarter and 7.8% from a year ago. Deals valued at $10M or more accounted for more than two-thirds of total dollar volume, and the data suggests that deals are starting to concentrate in higher-priced, larger assets. “Industrial and office trades drove the momentum through the third quarter, despite the rise in interest rates,” Cole Perry, associate director of research at Altus Group, said in a statement. “While the shift toward larger transactions suggests capital is becoming more willing to move when investors see quality and conviction in the opportunity.” The last few months have included shake-ups to the capital markets landscape that will test the resilience of CRE demand in the fourth quarter. Yields for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds first cleared 5% in September , shortly before the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time since 2023. Shares of tech stocks in the booming world of artificial intelligence were already slumping before the bombshell ouster of Jensen Huang , Nvidia ’s former CEO and one of the most prolific voices in the AI race, earlier this month pushed them down further.
