items.title: A sluggish housing market has held back Home Depot. Here's Cramer's advice on the stock now
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Jim Cramer said Home Depot's latest earnings report strengthened his confidence in the retailer's long-term prospects. He pointed to improving demand and market-share gains as reasons to buy the dip, arguing that Home Depot is well-positioned to benefit from an eventual housing recovery. CNBC's Jim Cramer said that Home Depot's third-quarter earnings report strengthened his confidence in the retailer's long-term prospects, rendering the stock's pullback Tuesday a buying opportunity. "I told CNBC Investing Club members today that, if we weren't restricted in the name, I would be buying today's dip and adding more Home Depot shares for my Charitable Trust," the " Mad Money " host said. "This was a good quarter, and the negative response just seems to be based on a myopic view of what the company was implying about the current quarter with its updated guidance." Shares of the home improvement retailer fell 2% despite reporting better-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue. Same-store sales climbed 2.2%, marking the retailer's strongest comps performance in four years. The sell-off appeared driven by updated full-year guidance that implied slightly weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter results. But Cramer cautioned against reading too much into the forecast, noting Home Depot's history of conservative guidance, particularly as it prepares for a leadership transition. The company announced Tuesday that veteran CFO Richard McPhail will succeed Ted Decker as CEO next week. Decker, who went on temporary medical leave in August, will continue to serve as chair of the board. Home Depot shares have struggled to gain traction in recent years, as elevated interest rates weighed on housing activity and home improvement spending. Higher mortgage rates have discouraged homeowners from moving, reducing demand for the renovation projects that often accompany home sales. Shares have shown signs of life since reaching a 52-week low on Oct. 1, rallying roughly 20%, as bond yields retreated and investors rotated into consumer stocks. Still, the stock remains down 1% for the year. But Cramer argued that Home Depot's latest results offer reasons to own the stock while waiting for a decline in interest rates to spark a meaningful inflection for the business. "I heard enough from management to stay invested now, and I feel even better about the long-term prospects of Home Depot after today's report," he said. On the earnings call, incoming CEO McPhail highlighted strength in the repair and remodeling businesses, while 13 of Home Depot's 16 product categories posted positive comparable sales and online sales continued growing at a double-digit pace. Cramer said those encouraging demand trends, along with market-share gains among professional contractors, suggest Home Depot is strengthening its business even before the housing market recovers. "For those with a long-term view, the important part is that the company is taking share," he said. "Whenever the broader housing market does return, Home Depot is positioned to be one of the companies that stands to benefit the most." items.title: Pending Home Sales Fall in October As Rates Hit 2026 Peak
items.description: Pending Home Sales Fall in October As Rates Hit 2026 Peak By Hannah Jones Nov 18, 2026 What did pending home sales look like in October? Pending home sales fell to another record-low, easing 4.7% in October, as mortgage rates hit a recent peak of 7.4%, and were down 16.7% from a year earlier. Rates have since eased back into the low 7% range, but October’s hot inflation data , released last week, is likely to push them higher again. Headline inflation rose 0.4% month over month, well above the 0.2% to 0.3% forecast, and core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. Markets now expect that a Fed rate hike is coming in December. Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued. What does this mean for buyers, sellers, and the housing market? All four regions saw declines both month over month and year over year, led by the West, where contract signings fell 6.9% for the month and 20.3% from a year earlier. The South followed with declines of 6.3% and 18.7%, then the Midwest with 2.7% and 14.0%. The Northeast had the smallest monthly drop, 0.8%, but was still down 11.1% from a year earlier. Even though all four regions saw dramatic cooling, the relative strength of the Midwest and Northeast are clear, due largely to still-scarce inventory conditions. Though all large metros saw pending home sales ease annually, the smallest drops were in Cincinnati (-4.7%), Austin (-9.7%) and Hartford, CT (-10.0%). Did the run-up to the November midterms keep buyers on the sidelines? Possibly. Some home shoppers may have held off to wait for the results, but rising rates are the more likely culprit . Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment. That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb. Affordability remains the limiting factor in today’s housing market. The typical mortgage-holder would see a $1,100 increase in their monthly payment if they bought a median-priced home today. Sellers have shown some flexibility, with lower asking prices and more price cuts , but buyers have not responded with much enthusiasm at these rates. Sellers are only willing to come down so far and buyers are only willing to stretch so far, and a gap still separates the two. As a result, transaction volume in October hit its lowest level in 16 years . There is an upside for buyers who can afford to act. With fewer shoppers in the market, they will face less competition for each listing, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more willing to negotiate on price, repairs, or closing costs.

items.title: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid
items.description: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid The rule could displace tens of thousands of people, housing organizations say. A lawsuit claims the change is illegal and unconstitutional. Published Nov. 18, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google A U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule finalized Nov. 12, 2026, requires tenants receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 2 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development finalized a rule Nov. 12 requiring households receiving federal housing assistance to provide proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for all household members. The rule, which goes into effect Dec. 14, effectively ends prorated federal housing assistance, which based the level of assistance on the number of eligible family members in the household. The new regulation could impact housing assistance for as many as 80,000 people, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A lawsuit challenging the rule’s legality was filed in the U.S. Central District of California Monday. Dive Insight: Nearly 9 million people participate in HUD housing assistance programs, which have long required immigration eligibility, according to NLIHC. HUD said the rule aims to bolster the agency’s “enforcement of the law” by requiring verification of immigration status for all household residents. It asserts that providing assistance to mixed-status households reduces the funds available to households that are fully eligible. “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said Nov. 10 in a press release. The agency said an audit of HUD-assisted households found around 200,000 tenants “ with incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.” David Dworkin, president and CEO of the National Housing Conference, called the regulation “a step backward.” “HUD’s concerns about immigration should be addressed through enforcement of existing laws, not by effectively evicting families who are here legally and creating expensive and burdensome processes for housing providers that are not capable of immigration enforcement,” Dworkin said in a statement. Of the approximately 80,000 individuals who could be displaced by the new requirements, nearly half are children, according to NLIHC. The lawsuit was filed by three unnamed plaintiffs residing in public housing or receiving housing assistance in Los Angeles County and two Los Angeles-area housing advocacy groups. It alleges the rule violates the Fair Housing Act, the Administrative Procedures Act and the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment guarantee of due process rights. items.title: Nearly Nine in 10 Columbus-Area Residents Call Housing Affordability a Serious Problem, New Survey Finds
items.description:
Nearly Nine in 10 Columbus-Area Residents Call Housing
           Affordability a Serious Problem, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Columbus-area residents
COLUMBUS, Ohio – November 18, 2026 – Nearly nine in 10 Columbus-area residents say housing
affordability is a serious problem, and more than half have considered moving because of housing costs,
according to a new survey. Yet fewer than one in four are aware that Congress recently passed federal
legislation, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built
single-family rental homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: Nearly 90% of Columbus-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 55% have considered moving because of housing costs,
       including 30% who have considered leaving Ohio altogether.
   ●   Essential workers are feeling it: 63% say it is hard for teachers, nurses, police officers and
       firefighters to afford to live in the communities where they work.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 69% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   A majority of residents support new rental housing: 57% of Columbus-area residents support
       building more rental homes, 2-to-1 over those opposed.
   ●   Renters choose community over commute: By more than four to one, Columbus renters would
       rather rent a single-family home in the community they want than buy a larger home farther from
       work and family (46% to 10%). Two-thirds support building more single-family rentals to make
       that possible.

“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman, CEO
of the National Rental Home Council.

The findings come as Ohio policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following federal action
this past summer. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act authorized several new programs,
streamlined existing programs, like the HOME grant program, and placed limits on large institutional
investors from purchasing existing single-family homes.

“As state policymakers look ahead to 2027,” Todman said, “the opportunity is to help families find a home
that works for them, close to the jobs and communities they’ve built their lives around.”

About the survey

The survey of 600 Columbus-area residents was conducted via Pollfish in October 2026.

items.title: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER
items.description: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER Single-family leasing activity increased as rental prices edged higher HOUSTON -- (November 18, 2026) -- Houston-area renters kept the market moving in October, leasing more homes than a year ago even as rental prices edged higher. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Rental Market Update, 3,850 single-family homes were leased, a 3.5% increase from 3,720 in October 2025. A healthy supply of rental homes helped keep prices relatively stable. The average lease price for a single-family home rose just 1.2% to $2,293, compared to $2,266 in October 2025. "With affordability still top of mind, many people are taking a closer look at their housing options and what works best for their budgets," said HAR Chair-Elect Kat Robinson with SERHANT. "As we head toward the end of the year, that will continue to play a big role in whether people decide to rent or buy. For renters, it's encouraging to see that prices haven't changed much from last year." Townhomes and condominiums also saw an increase in leasing activity. A total of 638 properties were leased in October, up 9.1% from 585 a year earlier. The average lease price rose 4.0% to $1,943, while the median price increased 2.9% to $1,800. Rental inventory in this segment continued to expand. New listings increased 1.7% to 1,143 properties, while active listings rose 3.3% to 2,387. Townhomes and condominiums spent an average of 48 days on the market, one day longer than a year ago. items.title: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook
items.description: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook Written by Kenny Lee on November 18, 2026 What happened Housing starts jumped 9.9% from September to 1.309 million SAAR in October, up 2.8% from September last year. While starts in the West fell to the lowest in more than six years, the Midwest and South showed strength, rising 48.4% and 10.5%, respectively. However, sharp declines in new-construction permits indicate builders’ caution. Authorized units declined 7.4% to 1.295 million in October, with the single-family segment down sharply by 8.7%. All four Census regions saw declines in single-family construction permits. While notoriously volatile, multifamily housing starts nationwide jumped 25.5% to 433 thousand units in October. Although multifamily permits fell 5.2% from September to 475 thousand units in October, the latest pace is an improvement from this summer. Compared to last year, the three-month moving average of multifamily permits was up 3.5% from a year ago. Why it matters Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October , the largest year-over-year drop since 2023. Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes , the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane. The flipside of cooling buyer demand is skyrocketing renter demand. As elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead, renter demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Although the industry has been grappling with high new construction inventory over the past few years since the construction boom in 2022 and 2023, recent Zillow data shows market fundamentals started improving this year. The typical multifamily rent increased 2.5% year over year in October, compared to 1.3% growth one year ago, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Stronger rent growth reflects a resurgence of renter demand across the country. Recent gains in multifamily permits could be an early sign that the supply outlook is transitioning to growth. That said, it is worth noting that the Census Bureau's multifamily construction data relies on a survey with a small sample and is often subject to large revisions, and it will take additional data to see whether the recent gains indicate a new trend. Although developers still face challenging market conditions, such as high costs of construction financing, building materials, and skilled labor, a sustained improvement in multifamily supply will help alleviate the pressure on renters. items.title: November 2026 Commercial Real Estate Market Insights Report
items.description: Commercial Real Estate Market Insights November 2026 Commercial Real Estate Market Insights Report Share Download the report pdf (1.55 MB) Economic growth continued in September, although hiring slowed and inflation picked up. Consumer and business spending remained strong. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point, while long-term Treasury yields also rose. Higher borrowing costs continued to affect commercial real estate investment and refinancing activity. Commercial real estate continued to improve in September, although conditions varied across property types. Some sectors improved further, while others remained mostly steady. Below is a summary of the performance of each major commercial real estate sector in September of 2026: The office sector continued its gradual recovery in the third quarter, supported by strengthening demand and improving occupancy trends. Sustained positive absorption and firmer rent growth suggest that market conditions are becoming more constructive, although substantial excess inventory continues to limit the pace of recovery. Class A led demand despite elevated vacancy, while Class B saw moderating tenant losses. Class C maintained the lowest vacancy despite continued move-outs. Multifamily fundamentals strengthened in the third quarter, supported by resilient demand and slowing new supply. Absorption outpaced deliveries, helping reduce excess inventory, ease vacancy, and support gradual rent growth, although pricing power remains constrained. With the construction pipeline at a decade low, supply pressures could moderate further. Class A benefited from a favorable supply-demand balance, while Class B maintained steady demand and improving fundamentals. Class C returned to positive absorption and retained the lowest vacancy among classes. Improving demand supported the retail sector in the third quarter, narrowing the supply-demand gap while vacancy held near historic lows. Despite deliveries exceeding absorption, tight availability helped sustain pricing conditions, although rent growth moderated. General retail led demand and maintained the lowest vacancy, while Neighborhood Centers, Malls, and Power Centers returned to positive absorption. Neighborhood and Power Centers recorded the strongest rent growth, though new supply could place modest upward pressure on vacancy. The industrial sector made further progress toward rebalancing in the third quarter as stronger demand narrowed the gap with new supply. Improving absorption is helping reduce excess inventory, although elevated vacancy and restrained rent growth continue to limit the recovery. Logistics remained the primary driver of demand, while specialized facilities maintained the lowest vacancy. Flex continued to lag, recording further tenant move-outs and the highest vacancy among major industrial property types. Conditions across the hospitality sector showed limited change in September, with occupancy still below pre-pandemic levels amid persistent weakness in corporate travel and the impact of remote work. ADR and RevPAR continued to exceed 2019 levels, supporting operating performance despite softer occupancy. Meanwhile, elevated financing costs and economic uncertainty continued to constrain investment activity and temper investor interest. Back to top

items.title: The Market Dynamics of November: Sales, Inventory, and Buyer Trends
items.description: The Market Dynamics of November: Sales, Inventory, and Buyer Trends November 12, 2026 Residential Real Estate By: Chris Lux Share Fall is in full swing, and the autumnal mindset is becoming more noticeable in your day-to-day decisions. The fleece-lined jacket is starting to appear on the way to work, and the time shift makes the drive home feel like the day is essentially over. Plans to visit family are beginning to materialize, and the dread of another uncomfortable “discussion” with the extended family has many prospective buyers distracted from searching for a new home and moving forward with the move, resulting in a slower market heading into the holiday season. These are what we call seasonality trends, patterns we see every year around the same time. They help explain how buyers and sellers usually behave as the housing market enters the fall season and offer useful insight for planning real estate strategies. Buyers and sellers can use these seasonal trends to understand the broader market as they decide when to buy or list their home. The following estimates represent a “normal” pre-pandemic fall (1999-2019). This allows us to compare today’s housing market with what is typically expected at this time of year. Supply & Demand To begin, we can look at the average non-seasonally adjusted month-over-month percentage change in existing-home sales in November. Historically, about 399,000 existing home sales occur in November, a notable decrease from October: • October: -0.9% • November: -9.6% • December: 3.9% • January: -27.2% Existing-home sales typically decline by about 9.6% in November, representing a substantial shift and the third-largest average monthly reduction. The effects of fall weather are now fully present in many regions, and holiday busyness, coupled with the fact that school and activities have picked up for children, makes November a more complicated time to move than October. While sales are typically at their lowest in the last quarter of the year, they remain substantially higher than in the peak winter months on average, highlighting the effect of frigid temperatures on transaction volume. Shifting to inventory, we can look at the percentage change in supply to better understand buyers' position in November relative to sellers' listing decisions around this time of year. Historically, about 2.4 million existing homes are available for sale in November. This level reflects the pre-pandemic fall conditions, well above today’s inventory, which remains around 1.6 million – about 800,000 homes short of what used to be normal: • October: -1.0% • November: -2.7% • December: -9.4% • January: 0.6% Historically, inventory declines by about 2.7% in November, just behind December, as the second-largest month-to-month decrease in supply on average. Similar to buyers, sellers likely experience sluggishness going into the colder months and may be reluctant to move due to the lack of offers being made in their local markets. Sellers may expect that listing a home in November could result in a December move, which would bring various challenges associated with moving around the new year, along with a higher likelihood of snow and added complications, especially if it requires long-distance travel. https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30775441/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script Prices tend to change little in November, with a slight average increase of 0.2%. This reflects a change in the median price of homes sold and may also reflect the mix of homes available during the period. Days on the Market: How Quickly Sellers Can Expect to Find a Buyer Next, we will look at how long a typical home stays on the market to see how November market conditions affect the time it takes a seller to find a deal in the late fall season. https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30775444/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script The number of days a typical home spends on the market tends to increase by 2 days in November. This increase is relatively small compared to the spikes seen in early fall, suggesting that September and October mark the initial transition out of the busy season, which continues into November. Although there is less daylight in November, the larger spikes associated with adverse weather have yet to set in, making November relatively similar to October in terms of the time required to find a buyer. Buyer Characteristics: Who is in the Market in November? Lastly, we will look at the share of first-time and cash buyers to get a sense of the typical buyer in November. The share of first-time home buyers typically declines by 0.7 percentage points in November, putting it in line with late spring and late summer. Now that the school year is in full swing, first-time buyers with young children may be reluctant to move since it would mean uprooting children that have settled into a classroom. Despite this inconvenience, some first-time buyers may expect that finding a home during winter will be particularly difficult due to low inventory and adverse weather, leading them to prioritize a move before winter sets in. Cash buyers tend to increase by about 0.7 percentage points in November, making it the most prominent fall month for this demographic and the highest share since March. Cash buyers are likely to be more active when prices are lower than in other months. While prices do see a slight increase in November, the minimal change, coupled with the consecutive decreases typically seen in early fall, may encourage some cash buyers to move before demand spikes in December, as many households push to get into a new home before the end of the year. In November, REALTORS® can expect a slowdown in activity as households plan for the holidays and year-end. Existing-home sales (not seasonally adjusted) were 341,000 in September, down 4.7% from August. This is typical around this time of year, as the school year kicks off and families face more logistical challenges heading into fall. However, when we compare the percentage decrease in 2026 to pre-pandemic levels, it appears there was a much softer fall slowdown than is typically seen around this time of year. From 1999 to 2019, sales fell an average of about 15% from August to September, about 3 times less activity than what was seen this year. But September’s smaller drop does not mean the seasonal cooling has faded. From July through September, sales fell about 15% this year compared with an average of 13% from 1999 to 2019. In other words, it seems that the fall slowdown started earlier this year. August Was the Unusual Month Sales fell 10.7% from July to August, the largest decrease over this period since at least 1999. Historically, August sales tend to increase by 2.6% on average. This happened largely due to mortgage rates. Rates fell to about 6% in February and March, the lowest level since 2022, which boosted activity in late spring and early summer. In June, sales reached 424,000, up 8% from a year earlier. However, as rates moved back up to about 6.7% over the summer, sales cooled earlier than usual. This is not the first time rates have shifted the timing of the seasonal pattern. In 2023, rates rose over the summer, and sales decreased even earlier (in July). In 2024, rates peaked at about 7% in the spring, and June sales fell instead of experiencing the typical spike. However, when rates dropped to about 6.2% in September, October sales rose. Thus, the seasonal pattern remains, but in today’s market, the data shows that its timing is increasingly tied to mortgage rates. Inventory Kept Rising Another key difference between the two periods is recognized in the supply side. Inventory increased by 1.9% to 1.60 million in September, while historically it tends to decline by about 2.6% from August to September. This was the highest September inventory level since 2019, giving buyers more options as sales activity slowed. However, inventory is still about 12% below September 2019; and relative to the pace of sales, supply is about 4.7 months. Prices Follow a Typical Pattern Unlike sales and inventory, home prices aligned with a more typical seasonal pattern. The median price declined by 2.4% from August to September to $417,500, on par with the historical average reduction of about 2.6%. Prices usually ease in the fall as fewer higher-priced family homes sell after the school year begins. Compared to a year earlier, the median price was up 1.3%, one of the smallest year-over-year gains in September in more than a decade. Key Takeaways for Buyers and Sellers Looking ahead, mortgage rates rose from about 6.7% in early September to 7.4% in October. While this hasn't yet been reflected in closed sales, we can look at the last time rates rose significantly to gauge the potential effect. In the fall of 2023, sales activity decreased by about 15% from September to December following a jump in rates, reflecting about twice the typical decline. In light of this, we may expect the coming months to be slower than usual. For buyers who are financially ready, this may be a good time to shop. There are more homes to choose from than at any other point since 2020, and with less competition, there can be more opportunities for price negotiation or concessions. For sellers, pricing the home right from the start and being open to negotiation will matter more as homes take longer to sell. While many factors can impact sales levels in a particular month, it is important to consider how current market conditions can amplify or suppress the trends we tend to see as the seasons change. With relatively low inventory and sales compared to historic levels, coupled with mortgage rates above 7%, prospective buyers are likely to be more flexible with their timing, especially if affordability improves. Based on recent data, the housing market still follows its usual seasonal rhythm; however, the fall slowdown arrived a month earlier than expected. As we have seen, mortgage rates can influence buyers' timing and will likely shape how the rest of the year unfolds. Chris Lux Chris Lux is an economist for the National Association of REALTORS®. items.description: Top 10 Takeaways from NAR’s 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers November 5, 2026 Residential Real Estate , Being a Real Estate Professional , Being an Agent , Working With Buyers , Working With First-Time Homebuyers By: Jessica Lautz Share Please note: The data visualization embeds on this page are best viewed on a laptop or desktop computer. The National Association of REALTORS® has been producing the Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers since 1981. Each report reflects a unique economic environment and an ever-changing real estate market. These were the most striking takeaways from this year’s report on who can enter a housing market plagued by limited affordable housing inventory and elevated mortgage interest rates. 1. First-time buyers : First-time home buyers increased slightly from the lowest historical share of 21% to 22% as housing affordability improved momentarily due to a short-lived drop in mortgage interest rates. First-time buyers continue to face limited affordable inventory and difficulty saving for a down payment. Before the Great Recession, 40% of primary residence buyers were 40% first-time buyers. Even among successful first-time buyers, the hardest step was finding the right property. While young adults still want the American Dream of homeownership, they feel priced out of achieving it. 2. Age of first-time buyers : The overall median age of first-time buyers remained at the all-time high seen in last year’s report of 40 years old. Since 2010, the age of first-time buyers has been incrementally climbing from 30. First-time home buyers are likely older because they have to save longer and are entering a market with limited inventory, which may require longer searches to find a home. Additionally, there is an important distinction between first-time buyers who financed versus those who made all-cash purchases. First-time buyers who financed had a median age of 38, while first-time buyers who made an all-cash purchase had a median age of 54. 3. All cash first-time buyers : First-time buyers who made all cash purchases rose to the highest level recorded of 10%. These all-cash buyers were more likely than financed buyers to obtain funds from a cash inheritance, an inherited property, or financial assets. 4. Age of repeat buyers : The age of repeat buyers also remains at an all-time high seen last year. In 1981, the median age of repeat buyers was 36. Today it is 62. Repeat buyers who decide to purchase are moving later in life, many of whom are likely retired, and their top reason for moving is to be close to friends and family. As the share of the population aged 65 and older grows, it is reasonable to assume more homeowners in this age group will make housing trades, along with the financial ability to do so. The lock-in effect of low-rate mortgages may be keeping younger homeowners in place. 5. Household composition : As marriage rates in the U.S. have continued to steadily decline to just 47%, there has been a shift in who is purchasing homes. This reflects all buyers, but is most pronounced among first-time home buyers. This year, just 47% of first-time home buyers were married, while 25% were single women, 12% were single men, and 11% were unmarried couples. First-time buyers purchasing as roommates were at a 45-year high of 5%. Purchasing as roommates has become an attractive option for buyers as it addresses housing affordability with dual incomes and companionship. 6. Multi-generational homes : Families continue to look for creative solutions to address family needs under one roof. Fourteen percent of home buyers purchased a multi-generational home. The main reasons are to accommodate aging parents, allow young adults to live at home, and save money. However, while those are the most common reasons, the share of home buyers with children under 18 who share a residence to reduce childcare costs jumped from 11% in 2025 to 16% in 2026. Childcare costs are also a growing concern among successful buyers and held back savings, increasing from 14% in 2025 to 17% in 2026 among buyers who had difficulty saving. 7. Length of Ownership Among Sellers : Home sellers have now owned their home for a median of 12 years before selling. This is an all-time high. The lock-in effect of low-interest-rate mortgages is likely contributing to longer home tenure. If a homeowner doesn't have a motivating reason to move, they stay put longer. Increased home tenure is likely driven by the age of home sellers and repeat buyers. If more repeat buyers are in their 60s, they may have owned a family home for many decades and are now at a point in their life where they are ready for a housing trade. 8. Neighborhood choice : Neighborhood choice and reason to purchase have changed considerably among home buyers in the last two decades. Buyers who chose a neighborhood that was convenient to their job are now at just 31 percent, down from 52 percent in 2014. Convenience to friends and family is up from a low of 35 percent in 2015 to 46 percent. Because retirees dominate the market, being close to one’s support system tends to outweigh everything else. 9. Buyer Use of Agent : Ninety percent of home buyers use a real estate agent or broker to purchase their home—the highest in four decades. Buyers want a real estate agent or broker who can help them find the right home, negotiate, and understand the real estate market. This is the biggest financial purchase of one’s life, and home buyers rely on real estate agents to achieve the American Dream. 10. items.description: Fur-Ever Home: Pets’ Spell on Homebuying Decisions October 27, 2026 Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Remodeling , Design & Architecture By: Amethyst Marroquin , Chris Lux Share Please note: The data visualization embeds on this page are best viewed on a laptop or desktop computer. Whether it's a black cat perched beside a cauldron or a loyal dog roaming a haunted neighborhood, pets have always been part of Halloween's charm. Pop culture has introduced us to iconic companions like Salem from “Sabrina the Teenage Witch” and the unforgettable pup Sparky from “Frankenweenie,” reminding us that even the spookiest stories need a faithful friend. While these iconic Halloween sidekicks may be fictional, the bond between people and their pets is very real. For many recent home buyers, pets are more than companions; they're family members whose needs can help shape important decisions during the home search. Cats may be known for keeping witches company, but pets of all kinds have become cherished members of American households. According to the American Pet Products Association , 95 million U.S. households owned at least one pet in 2025. It’s no surprise, then, that these companions influence everything from daily routines to major financial decisions, including where to live. And while 76% of all home buyers in 2025 had no children under the age of 18 living at home, pets are playing an even more central role in many home buyers’ lives and housing choices. One reason pets play such an important role is how much time owners spend with them. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ American Time Use Survey , Americans are spending more time with their pets than ever before. In 2025, 19.5% of Americans spent time with a pet on a given day, up from 13.7% in 2005. Among women, that share rose from 15.8% in 2005 to 23% over the same two decades. Americans spent an average of 0.74 hours with their pets in 2025, a 15% increase from 2005. As pets take on an increasingly important role in our lives, households are investing more in their care and well-being. As the days grow shorter and the spooky season settles in, it’s worth taking a step back to get a sense of the typical buyer and seller’s resolve going into the month of cooler weather and jumpscares around every corner. The housing market continues to face challenges as mortgage rates remain elevated. From January through September 2026, 3.09 million existing homes were sold, up 0.8% from the same period last year. This is down from the 1.6% year-to-date increase reported last month, which shows that the market is still struggling to gain momentum. Inventory, however, reached 1.6 million in September 2026 compared to just over 1.5 million in 2025, suggesting that sellers are a bit more willing to step into the unknown. Over the same period, home prices have risen by 1.3%. With the specter of affordability difficulties still looming over the market, buyers remain sensitive to mortgage rates. Since it typically takes one to three months for changes in mortgage rates to show up in closed sales, we may not see the full effect right away. Still, buyers have more homes to choose from, and for some, the longing looks their pets make when they see a full backyard may be enough to prioritize a home purchase. Just like Salem and Sparky were beloved companions in their tales, many pets play an important role in their owners’ lives. According to the 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers Report , 1% of recent home buyers shared their primary reason for purchasing a home was to provide a better home for their pets. Among these pet-focused buyers, more than half (52%) were married couples, 27% were single females, and 14% were unmarried couples. These buyers also tended to be older: Of those who said their primary reason for purchasing their home was to give their pet a better home, 37% are younger boomers (61 to 70 years old) and 24% are Gen Xers (46 to 60 years old). As children leave the nest and lifestyles evolve, many of these buyers may prioritize the comfort and well-being of their four-legged family members, suggesting that when it comes to finding the perfect home, pets can be just as influential as any human housemate for some buyers. Our pets may not sign the mortgage paperwork, but they have a surprisingly significant influence on the neighborhoods buyers ultimately choose. According to the 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers, 16% of recent buyers said that proximity to veterinary services and access to outdoor space for their pets were important considerations when selecting a neighborhood. Married repeat buyers (60%) and first-time single female buyers (28%) were especially likely to prioritize these pet-friendly features. For many households, choosing the right neighborhood means finding a community that works for every family member, including the four-legged ones. Beyond access to veterinary care and outdoor space, pet-minded buyers often looked for neighborhood amenities that make daily life more enjoyable for both owners and their companions. Buyers who considered their pets when selecting a neighborhood were more likely to prioritize nearby parks and recreation facilities (35% compared to 29% of those who did not consider pets), walkability (31% compared to 19%), and the availability of larger lots or acreage (26% compared to 16%). Whether it's a haunted hike through the neighborhood, a game of fetch in a nearby park, or a backyard large enough for a spirited round of zoomies, these features can be just as appealing to pets as they are to their owners. As Halloween falls upon us and neighborhood porches fill with jack-o’-lanterns, skeletons, ghosts, and the occasional black cat decoration, pets clearly occupy a special place in the homes and hearts of many Americans. items.description: The Market Dynamics of October: Sales, Inventory, and Buyer Trends October 21, 2026 Residential Real Estate By: Chris Lux Share The leaves are turning brown, the air is crisper with each passing day, and you are beginning to get settled into a comfortable routine as the holiday season approaches. This sentiment appears to be shared among many prospective buyers and sellers, as market activity tends to see a slight slowdown relative to September. Children are settled into the school year, and the recent shifts in temperature and daylight have some families choosing to remain in place. At the same time, other families may have noticed that there is less competition to get into homes, encouraging them to pursue a home purchase. Inclinations such as these can offset each other, which may explain the small changes seen in October; however, they signal larger shifts that tend to occur in the coming months as the year comes to an end. These are what we call seasonality trends, patterns we see every year around the same time. They help explain how buyers and sellers usually behave as the housing market enters the fall season and offer useful insight for planning real estate strategies. Buyers and sellers can use these seasonal trends to understand the broader market as they decide how to time their home purchase or listing. It is important to note that the following estimates represent a “normal” pre-pandemic fall (1999-2019). This allows us to compare today’s housing market with what would typically be expected during this time of year. Supply & Demand To begin with, we can look at the average month-over-month percentage change of existing-home sales in October. Historically, about 442,000 existing-home sales occur in October, which is slightly fewer than September: September: -15.4% October: -0.9% November: -9.6% December: 3.9% Historically, existing-home sales decrease by about 0.9% in October. This is the smallest reduction out of all the months on average, which suggests that October does not substantially differ from September. Buyers remain in an in-between period where it has become inconvenient to move due to the school year—yet not as logistically difficult as the winter months, which bring harsher weather and planning around the holidays. As such, buyers likely feel conflicted about moving at this time of year, resulting in little change in sales. Shifting to inventory, we can look at the percentage change in supply to better understand the position of buyers in October relative to the listing decisions of sellers around this time of year. Historically, about 2.5 million existing homes are available for sale in October. Similar to sales, this represents a small decrease compared to September. This level reflects the pre-pandemic fall conditions, well above today’s inventory, which remains around 1.6 million—about a million homes short of what used to be normal: September: -2.6% October: -1.0% November: -2.7% December: 9.4% Similar to sales, inventory typically declines by about 1.0% in October, the second smallest decline of the year. With lower prices relative to the summer coupled with the logistical challenges discussed above, many sellers likely feel less motivated to list their home. Additionally, sellers may expect that finding a buyer will be more challenging relative to what was seen in prior months, resulting in longer listing times. This could mean a move closer to Thanksgiving, which poses difficulties as families coordinate holiday plans. Despite this, sellers may sense that their momentum will slow down going into the winter, motivating them to complete a move now when the weather remains favorable so that they can be in a new home before the end of the year. The trend seen in sales and inventory continues with prices, which also tend to see a reduction of about 1.1% in October. The decrease is relatively low compared to the prior months, but the change represents where prices typically remain through the end of the year as little change is seen in the coming months. Despite the decline, prices remain higher in the fall compared to midwinter through early spring, suggesting the market requires more time to cool coming out of peak summer season, as the motivation to get into a new home before the end of the year sustains activity. Days on the Market: How Quickly Sellers Can Expect to Find a Buyer Next, we will look at the number of days a typical home remains on the market to see how market conditions in October impact the time required for a seller to find a deal in the fall season. The number of days a typical home spends on the market tends to rise by about four days in October, the largest increase since January. The incline represents a continuation of the market cooling that typically begins in September when sales levels see a distinct shift away from peak season. As such, the spike seen in October is likely a residual effect of the initial seasonal change marked by the beginning of the school year. Buyer Characteristics: Who Is in the Market in October? Lastly, we will look at the share of first-time and cash buyers to get a sense of the typical buyer in the month of October. In October, the share of first-time home buyers typically increases by 0.5 percentage points. The modest jump places October on a similar level to May and July when it comes to this demographic and represents the first increase since June. With fewer buyers in the market, first-time buyers may face less competition. items.title: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report
items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 18, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share Month-Over-Month 4.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 16.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions WASHINGTON (November 18, 2026) – Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” October 2026 National Pending Home Sales 4.7% decrease month-over-month 16.7% decrease year-over-year October 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 0.8% decrease month-over-month 11.1% decrease year-over-year Midwest 2.7% decrease month-over-month 14.0% decrease year-over-year South 6.3% decrease month-over-month 18.7% decrease year-over-year West 6.9% decrease month-over-month 20.3% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Cincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, IN (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, IL-IN (-11.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-12.7%) Jacksonville, FL (-12.8%) Cleveland, OH (-12.8%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. DOWNLOAD THE Q3 2026 REPORT Key Takeaways Life sciences employment across the Bay Area, according to Lightcast, ended the third quarter of 2026 at 104,400 positions, with some of the largest employers in the region being BioMarin Pharmaceutical, Amgen, and Gilead Sciences. Venture capital funding into Bay Area life sciences companies in the third quarter came in at $2.1 billion, according to Pitchbook. There was 828,511 sf of total leasing activity (new leases and renewals) for the third quarter, an increase from the 748,556 sf in the second quarter, and up from 783,364 sf during the same period last year. The overall average asking rate for Bay Area life sciences space closed out the third quarter at $5.53 psf on a monthly NNN basis, a decrease from $5.93 psf one year ago. Economic Overview Life sciences employment across the Bay Area, according to Lightcast, ended the third quarter of 2026 at 104,400 positions, with some of the largest employers in the region being BioMarin Pharmaceutical, Amgen, and Gilead Sciences. The Bay Area continues to be the top U.S. market in employment with Boston (101,900) and New York (87,000) following. Life sciences in the local region partially thrives from funding to universities from the National Institutes of Health (NIH); in the third quarter, Stanford ranked eighth while UCSF took the second spot, based on dollars awarded nationally. Venture capital funding into Bay Area life sciences companies in the third quarter came in at $2.1 billion, according to Pitchbook. During that period, Bay-Area headquartered companies received 28.0% of the total U.S. funding. The largest deals in the region went to San Francisco-based Chai Discovery at $400.0 million and South San Francisco-based Encoded at $275.0 million. Supply & Demand: Rising Vacancy in the East Bay The overall vacancy rate at the end of the third quarter of 2026 was 28.5%, down 20 basis points (bps) from 28.7% in the previous quarter and down 60 bps from 29.1% one year ago. Direct vacancy stayed relatively flat around 11.5 million square feet (msf). Sublease vacancy was consistent quarter-over-quarter as well at 2.5 msf. East Bay Oakland vacancy increased the most year-over-year, up 230 bps or 255,104 square feet (sf) from the same quarter last year, largely due to the delivery of new construction projects that completed in 2025. Additional consolidations also contributed to vacancy over the last 18 months. There was 828,511 sf of total leasing activity (new leases and renewals) for the third quarter, an increase from the 748,556 sf in the second quarter, and up from 783,364 sf during the same period last year. New leases made up 75.4% or 624,859 sf of the activity, while renewals made up the rest at 24.6% or 203,652 sf. New leases with Lilly Gateway Labs (South San Francisco) and Structure Therapeutics (South San Francisco) contributed significantly to activity this quarter. Supply: Eight Large-Scale Projects Completed in 2025 & 2026 There were eight ground-up developments, all speculative and totaling approximately 2.0 msf, completed since the beginning of 2025. These included Avia Labs (315,000 sf) in Millbrae, SPUR Phase I (330,350 sf) in South San Francisco, and The Landing (503,500 sf) in Burlingame. Along with those were 1030 Brittan Ave (108,134 sf) in San Carlos which was preleased to MBC Biolabs in 2022, Portal 405 (240,000 sf) in San Carlos, Menlo Park Labs (268,468 sf), and 200 Twin Dolphin (234,000 sf) in Redwood Shores. Finally, the last project that completed construction was ELCO Yards – The Shop in Redwood City, totaling 225,878 sf. Conversions were more active in the Bay Area in the third quarter with roughly 336,433 sf in the pipeline. Projects under renovation are 2400-2470 Charleston Road (108,474 sf) in Mountain View, Island Parkway (179,172 sf) in Redwood Shores, and 901 California Avenue (54,800 sf) in Palo Alto. items.title: New Home Lot Supply Index
items.description: New Home Lot Supply Index The New Home Lot Supply Index provides an unrivaled look into the lot markets across the country, offering a current quarter snapshot as well as insight into the directional trend. This report details data for the third quarter of 2026. November 18, 2026 – 4 min read Table of Content: Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index (LSI) for 3Q26, rose for the ninth consecutive quarter and showed lot supply loosened both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter across the United States. The index is a residential real estate indicator based on the number of single-family vacant developed lots (VDL) and the rate at which those lots are absorbed via housing starts. The New Home LSI came in at 88.5 for 3Q26, representing a 20.8% increase from 3Q25. This quarter, the market continued to be rated “appropriately supplied.” On a quarter-over-quarter basis, supply increased by 3.9% from 2Q26. The LSI counts the total vacant developed lot supply and adjusts it for overall starts activity. “The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” said Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market. Affordability pressures and widespread incentives underscore the challenges builders face in converting demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market means availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction; it does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost challenges have disappeared.” In 2Q26, the LSI sat right on the boundary between "slightly undersupplied" and "appropriately supplied." However, the upward movement in Q3 solidified the national rating as “appropriately supplied.” In 3Q26, lot supply loosened year-over-year across all major metropolitan areas Zonda tracks, except Boise. For markets that saw an increase in lot supply, the average year-over-year gain was significant at +32%. More markets trended up and were rated “appropriately supplied” or “oversupplied” in the third quarter, but 12 out of 30 were still categorized as “significantly undersupplied.” The markets where land supply loosened the most on a year-over-year basis were Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle. Boise was the only market where local lot supply tightened compared to 3Q25, falling from 65.7 to 51.9, joining one of 12 markets rated “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed ratings this quarter, as outlined in the chart below: Zonda also records future lots through the stages of development. The stages range from raw land through streets in, which is the last step before the lot becomes a vacant developed lot. Zonda groups the last few stages into a classification called total upcoming lots, which typically indicates delivery over the next 12-18 months. Total upcoming lots in 3Q26 increased 1.0% year-over-year and 1.6% quarter-over-quarter. These types of lots in the third quarter were down 12.2% from the 2022 peak but were up 23.4% compared to the same quarter in 2019. Among total upcoming lots, roadwork was down 15.3% year-over-year. Roadwork is comprised of the two smaller stages—streets paved and streets in—and represents the last step in lot development. Lots in the excavation stage were up 8.6% year-over-year, and those with equipment on site were up 5.7%. The largest share of total upcoming lots were in the excavation stage in 3Q26, totaling 416K. These lots have an expected delivery between 2Q27 and 3Q27 (the range represents different timeframes from local entitlement processes). Note, not all of the lots in excavation will match Zonda’s estimated timeline. “The development pipeline is edging higher, but the mix of activity matters,” Fergus said. “More lots are in excavation and equipment-on-site stages than a year ago, while fewer are in the final roadwork stages. That points to continued investment in future communities, but an uneven flow of near-term deliveries. Builders will need to weigh today’s softer demand environment against the time required to prepare lots for future construction.” Get a first look at Land AI Get a first look at Zonda Land AI on December 10th.
